open-question.question: Six of prompt 1's and three of prompt 2's deliberately-left-open items (team names, undoing an award, skipping a question, progress shown, keyboard control, reload survival; the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set at the start, answer validation) also appear as scored implied-requirement lines, so a minimal choice the prompt leaves open loses points on the implied axis. Where an item appears in both lists, which list keeps it: is it a scored implied line, an unscored open decision, or both with the overlap stated as intended?
open-question.alternative: Every item that appears in both lists, the nine named and any other overlap such as the tie on closeness and the team count, is removed from the prompt's "deliberately left open" list and stays a scored implied-requirement line unchanged; the draft extends line 33's one-list rule to the left-open and implied lists and states that a feature of the category is never a planted gap. No item is reworded. The implied axis keeps all thirteen and eleven lines and its claim to be as complete as the category allows, and no scored line is any longer called an open decision, so the contradiction with line 27's definition of a gap disappears with the least rewriting. Prompt 1's left-open list shrinks to roughly the qualities (difficulty, presentation, legibility) plus note-taking and the tie, and prompt 2's to two or three items, so the planted gaps that claim 1 and the review pass rely on thin out; and a minimal choice such as mouse-only or no team names is still scored as missing, now under the label of a convention, which a sceptic can still read as scoring taste.

Every overlapping item stays in the "deliberately left open" list and its implied-requirement line is deleted, so it is an unscored decision for the builder; the draft extends line 33's one-list rule and states that whether to have a feature the prompt leaves open is never scored. No item is reworded. No run loses points for a choice the stakeholder answers "your call" on, so the operator rule, line 27's definition of a gap, and "taste is not an axis" all hold, and the overlap can no longer be read as tilting the implied axis toward the questions Cairn's review pass raises. The implied axis loses six of prompt 1's thirteen lines and three of prompt 2's eleven, including strong conventions such as a reload not losing the game and a written set never overwriting the built-in questions, so the axis gets thinner and noisier and stops being as complete as the category allows.

Both lists stay as they are and the draft states the overlap as intended: the left-open list names questions to surface and the implied list scores what the category comes with, and a builder who settles a left-open item on the minimal answer is meant to lose the implied line. Line 27's definition of a gap and the taste section are rewritten so they no longer claim the two never overlap; gap 1 is recorded as rejected with that reason. Both purposes are kept at full strength with no list shrunk: the review pass still has every planted gap to find and the implied axis stays complete, and the text change is confined to stating the rule and its reason. The axis keeps rewarding more features on decisions the draft itself calls open, a run is graded on a preference the operator declined to state, and the overlap stays exactly what gap 1 says a sceptical reader will see as tilting the axis toward Cairn, now made explicit.

alternative.id: One list each by stated test

open-question.alternative: Every overlapping item goes to exactly one list, chosen item by item by a test the draft states (for example: an item is implied when a host-run quiz lacking it would be called broken or unfinished by any builder, and left open when lacking it is a defensible product choice); the draft records the verdict for each of the nine and any further overlap, so some stay scored (likely candidates such as reload survival or the built-in questions surviving) and others become unscored decisions (likely candidates such as team names or keyboard control). No item is reworded. Each item lands where it honestly belongs rather than by a blanket rule, so the strongest conventions stay scored while genuine product choices stop costing points, and the one-list rule holds with a reason a reader can re-apply. The test is itself a judgment applied by Cairn's author item by item, so borderline items (progress shown, answer validation) stay arguable and the sceptic's tilt objection moves from the lists to the verdicts; both lists shrink somewhat.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest implied

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split by what it decides: the implied line scores only that the host has some way through the case (as the implied axis already says, "what the way is does not matter"), and the left-open item is reworded to name only the choice among those ways (undo versus a confirmation before the award, skip versus revisit, resume versus a warning on reload, which keys drive the flow). An item with no such choice left once the feature exists (team names, progress shown, the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set) leaves the left-open list and stays a scored implied line. The draft states that the two lists may name the same feature only on these different scopes. The contradiction is removed while most planted gaps survive as real questions with several defensible answers, and the implied axis keeps every line, building on the "what the way is does not matter" rule the axis already states. Every overlapping item must be reworded and the reworded gaps are narrower, so a review pass may find them less often; and the whether-only items still score the minimal answer as missing, so gap 1's objection stands for team names, progress, and choosing a set.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest open

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split as in the whether-from-how split, the implied line scoring only that some way through exists and the left-open item reworded to the choice among ways; an item with no such choice left (team names, progress shown, the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set) keeps its left-open entry and its implied line is deleted, so it is unscored. The draft states that the two lists may name the same feature only on these different scopes. No whether-to-have-it decision is ever scored, so the operator's "your call" and the taste rule hold everywhere, while the case-handling lines (undo, skip, reload, validation) stay scored and the planted gaps stay numerous. Combines the rewording work of every split with the loss of several implied lines, among them the built-in questions surviving, which is arguably a plain convention of a question editor rather than a taste choice.

alternative.id: Split whether from how, rest by test

open-question.alternative: Each overlapping item is split as in the whether-from-how split wherever a choice among ways remains; each item with no such choice left goes to exactly one list by a test the draft states (implied when a quiz lacking it would be called broken or unfinished by any builder, left open when lacking it is a defensible product choice), with the verdict recorded per item. The draft states both rules. The most precise resolution: case-handling stays scored with its how left open, and only the whether-items are judged one by one, so each item's treatment can be defended on its own terms while the left-open list keeps the most planted gaps that are still genuine. The heaviest change, two rules and a per-item verdict for every overlap, and the verdicts on the whether-items remain judgments by Cairn's author, so the tilt objection survives in a narrower form.

open-question.question: The assess delivery differs from every manual delivery in two things at once, Cairn's structure and a planned stakeholder turn, and no manual delivery gets a planned turn, so the assess gain over manual cannot be attributed to Cairn alone. Does the benchmark add a manual delivery with a planned turn (the model lists the questions it needs answered, the operator answers them under the same disclosure rule, then the build instruction follows), and if so is it a primary delivery with a README row or an analysis-only control?
open-question.alternative: No manual delivery gets a planned turn, now or in this milestone. The draft keeps the four primary deliveries as they are and states the limitation instead. Comparing assess against a manual delivery mixes Cairn's structure with the stakeholder turn. YOLO against its multi-prompt control is the comparison attributed to Cairn's structure, since neither has a planned turn. Assess against YOLO is attributed to the turn under Cairn. The effect of a turn without Cairn stays unmeasured, and the page claims nothing that depends on it. No new delivery, operator input form, model-strategy key, or README row is added. The two decompositions the draft already has (YOLO against multi-prompt, assess against YOLO) each differ in one thing only, so the attribution rule holds once the overreaching comparison is stated as mixed rather than repaired. The top row of the ranking table (assess) still sits directly above manual rows that differ from it in two things, and a reader comparing them gets no separation. Headless sessions rarely end by asking, so a manual run almost never reaches the hidden knowledge, and the hidden-axis margin over manual stays partly a measure of having a turn at all, which the page can only caveat.

Add a fifth delivery, such as manual_clarify_then_build, defined like an ablation and kept off the page. Its first invocation asks the model to read PROJECT.md and list the questions it needs answered before building. That is followed by a planned operator turn: its input is the prompt text plus the model's list, it applies the same disclosure rule, and its reply is sent into the resumed session. Then comes the usual pointer-sentence build instruction in the same resumed session. Its scenario knowledge is the manual one: reply in plain prose. It runs in every comparison set and is reported in the analysis output, with no README table row and no radar curve. It measures the turn-without-Cairn effect that separates "Cairn surfaced the right question" from "the run got to ask", so the assess gain over manual can be split in the analysis. The page stays at four primary deliveries and four curves, as the radar's "four curves and never more" rule requires. The separation lives only in the analysis output. A reader of the landing page still sees assess above manual rows with the turn folded in, so the page's comparison still mixes the two causes, and every set pays for one more scenario that the page never shows. How much the listing step earns on the hidden axis depends on the sibling question's test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement, since a list of questions invites a catch-all.

Add the same clarify-then-build delivery (a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session, with the manual scenario knowledge) as a fifth primary delivery. It gets its own README table rows. On the radar it joins the single-prompt manual family, so the "manual prompt" curve is drawn from whichever of manual_prompt and manual_clarify_then_build ranks higher. The radar keeps four curves. The comparison the page leads with becomes honest on the page itself. A manual configuration that also gets a stakeholder turn has its own row, with its cost and its two attentive sessions per prompt beside it, and the manual curve is drawn from the strongest manual configuration, the turn included, so Cairn's margin is read against it. The page grows a row per manual strategy. The radar's manual curve may switch between a turn-less and a turn-bearing scenario from one set to the next, so the curve's meaning shifts and only the line under the chart says which it was. The table's rule of four primary deliveries is rewritten. As with every option that adds the turn, its hidden-axis value depends on the sibling test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement.

Add the clarify-then-build delivery (a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session, with the manual scenario knowledge) as a fifth primary delivery with its own README table rows. It also gets its own family and its own radar curve, raising the radar from four curves to five. The page shows the decomposition directly. The gap between the manual-with-turn curve and the plain manual curve is what a turn buys without Cairn. The gap between the assess curve and the manual-with-turn curve is what Cairn's structure adds when both get a turn, which is the comparison the attribution rule asks for. It overturns the draft's "four curves and never more" rule, and five overlapping curves on three axes are harder to read. Every comparison set gets one more primary scenario to run and rate before the page may be regenerated. The curve's hidden-axis value depends on the sibling test for when a question bears on a hidden requirement.

Add no fifth delivery. Redefine manual_prompt itself as clarify-then-build: a listing invocation, a planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answering into the resumed session, then the pointer-sentence build instruction in that session. Manual_prompt stays one of the four primary deliveries, with its README rows and its radar curve unchanged in place. The plain one-shot manual delivery is retired as a primary delivery. The page keeps four deliveries and four curves, and the one manual delivery the headline comparison reads against now has a planned turn like assess. The assess-against-manual comparison then differs in Cairn's structure only, with no extra scenario to run. The baseline of plain one-shot prompting, the way manual prompting is mostly used, disappears from the page. YOLO, which has no planned turn, is now read against a manual delivery that has one, so the YOLO-against-manual comparison mixes the two causes in the opposite direction. The manual multi-prompt control still has no turn.

Add no new delivery family. Extend the multi-prompt control's mirror rule so that the control derived from an assess scenario gets a counterpart to the turn. At the mirrored position, one invocation asks the model to list the questions it needs answered about PROJECT.md and the work so far. A planned operator turn under the same disclosure rule answers into that resumed session. The fixed continuation messages then follow as before, so N and the per-line model pairs still match the assess list. Controls mirroring a turn-less cairn scenario such as YOLO stay as they are. The control keeps its primary README rows and its multi-prompt radar family. The assess scenario's own control then differs from it in Cairn's structure only: same message count, same per-line pairs, same planned turn at the same position. The attribution is made within the comparison the draft already defines, with no fifth delivery and no fifth curve. It breaks the mirror rule that a control copies the planned messages only and can never drift. The listing invocation is a message with no cairn counterpart, so either N or the message at that position no longer matches. The two multi-prompt controls (mirroring YOLO and mirroring assess) now differ in kind under one family name. The single-prompt manual baseline still gets no turn.

open-question.question: The operator discloses a hidden requirement in reply to any question whose answer the statement changes, which a catch-all such as "anything else I should know before I start?" satisfies, so the hidden axis can reward a vague closing question rather than a surfaced one. What test decides that a question bears on a hidden requirement?

After each invocation the harness hands the final message to the operator; a message that asks gets a reply while one that reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer, gets none, but nothing says who makes that classification, and it is not recorded. How is the reply-or-no-reply classification of a final message made and recorded?
open-question.alternative: Every final message, a resumed session's included, goes to the operator itself, whose guideline states the reply rule; its output is either a reply or one fixed no-reply line carrying a one-clause reason. No harness rule runs first. Every such call writes its record file, the no-reply ones included, with the closing line stating the verdict and the reason. A no-reply verdict is not an operator turn: it adds no attentive session and no reply to the cap, and its tokens join the operator's own figures, kept apart from the scenario's totals. Needs no new component or versioned input: the one model already defined as the stakeholder makes the judgment a stakeholder would make, under the operator definition the manifest already pins, and every verdict lands in the record file the draft already keeps. The judge holds the hidden knowledge, so a borderline closing offer may be read as a question it can answer, which ties the hidden axis to how the operator reads ambiguity rather than to what the session asked; it also costs one operator call per invocation, about a dozen per cairn chain against one per manual run.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, and a match is a no-reply verdict with no model call, recorded as the matched line; every other message goes to the operator, which replies or outputs the fixed no-reply line with a one-clause reason, as in the operator-classifies option. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn, adds no attentive session, and the operator's tokens stay apart from the totals. A cairn chain's ordinary invocations are classified deterministically and for free, so model judgment and the operator's cost are spent only on messages that are genuinely open, which is every manual run's final message and any cairn message outside the fixed set. Viable only as far as Cairn fixes the wording of its no-op and stop lines, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns; the two families are classified by different means, a cairn message by rule and a manual one by judgment, and the judged path still lets the holder of the hidden knowledge decide.

A distinct model call, with no tools and a fixed model and effort pair, defined and versioned with the operator definition and recorded in the manifest, reads only the final message under a stated rule (asks, confirms, or offers a choice: reply; reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer: no reply) and outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason. It never sees the prompt or the hidden knowledge. Only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict and reason goes into the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; the classifier's tokens are recorded beside the operator's, apart from the totals. The judgment is made blind to the hidden knowledge and to the prompt, so whether a session receives a reply depends on what its message says alone, never on whether the stakeholder holds something it could disclose. Adds a second model input to version, pin, and keep identical across a comparison set, plus a call on every invocation of every scenario, and its stated rule still has to settle the offer-closing-with-a-question case the draft leaves fuzzy.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, a match being a no-reply verdict with no model call; every other message goes to the separate blind classifier of the separate-classifier option, which outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason, and only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; classifier tokens stay apart from the totals. Combines the deterministic, cost-free handling of every fixed Cairn line with a judgment that never sees the hidden knowledge, so the only model-classified messages are the open ones and their classification cannot lean toward disclosure. The most moving parts: a line table that must track Cairn's fixed wording, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns, plus a second versioned model input; cairn and manual messages are still classified by different means.

No model classifies. The harness applies one stated textual rule to every final message: a message matching one of Cairn's fixed status or stop lines gets no reply, and any other message gets a reply exactly when its last paragraph ends in a question mark. The verdict and the rule clause that produced it are written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session. Fully reproducible and free: the same message always gets the same verdict on any machine and under any operator version, so the classification adds no noise of its own to the hidden axis or the attentive-session count. A textual rule misreads exactly the case the question is about: an offer phrased as a question ("Want me to add tests?") gets a reply and a request phrased as a statement ("Let me know which you prefer.") gets none, so manual runs' route to the hidden knowledge turns on punctuation; it also depends on the fixed-line wording the fixed-stop-line question owns.

The draft keeps the reply rule as written, naming no classifier and recording no verdict; the gap is rejected in the text with the reason that the classification is a harness implementation detail, and the record files stay one per operator turn, so a no-reply message leaves no trace beyond the invocation output. Adds nothing to the design or to a run's cost and leaves the harness's author free to choose the mechanism when the harness is built. Whether a session receives a reply, and with it a manual run's only route to the hidden knowledge, stays an unstated and unrecorded judgment that can differ between implementations and runs, so a hidden-axis difference cannot be traced to it after the fact.

open-question.question: Every invocation loads the user-level configuration beside the plugin under test (other plugins, MCP servers, hooks, settings); the pre-flight checks only that Cairn is not installed at user level, and the manifest's user_config digests can detect a change but cannot recreate the configuration on another machine. How is the host configuration a run executes under isolated from the maintainer's own and made reproducible?
open-question.alternative: Isolation: none. Every invocation keeps loading the maintainer's user-level configuration (other plugins, MCP servers, hooks, settings, user CLAUDE.md) as the draft has it now. Reproducibility: the manifest keeps its user_config digests only. The draft's "Clearing memory" bullet, which says the content is recorded so a re-run can reproduce it, is rewritten to say instead that a run is reproducible only under the same user-level configuration, and the digests only detect a change. No harness, input, or credential work at all, and the draft stops promising a reproduction its manifest cannot deliver. Whatever the maintainer has installed loads into every scenario, so a plugin, hook, or MCP server can interact differently with Cairn's long multi-skill chain than with a single manual prompt, which is a difference between scenarios attributed to nothing they define; and nobody on another machine can rerun a set, which makes the published results unreproducible by design.

Isolation: none; the maintainer's user-level configuration keeps loading into every invocation. Reproducibility: the manifest's digests are replaced, or joined, by a copy of the effective user-level configuration kept in the run's unpublished record half: the user CLAUDE.md, the settings files, the list of enabled plugins with their versions or commits, and the configured MCP servers and hooks, so a later re-run can rebuild the same configuration from the record. Makes the draft's existing promise that the configuration's content is recorded true, without changing how a run executes or what credentials it needs. The confound stays: the maintainer's personal plugins and hooks still act on every run, Cairn and manual alike, and may not act equally; the copied settings and MCP entries can hold tokens or private paths that then live in the benchmark repository; and recreating third-party plugins and MCP servers at a recorded version is not always possible later.

Isolation: the maintainer's own config directory stays in use, but every invocation the harness makes (first form and resume form alike) adds flags that shut out the user's extensions: --strict-mcp-config with an empty MCP configuration, and --setting-sources restricted so user-level settings (and with them the plugins and hooks they enable) do not load; the flags are harness flags, set in exactly one place as the draft already requires for every non-strategy flag. The pre-flight gains a check that the flags are accepted by the host binary in use. Reproducibility: the flags are versioned with the harness; whatever user-level material the flags do not cover (such as the user CLAUDE.md, user-level skills or agents directories, output styles) is recorded by content in the unpublished record. Removes the bulk of the confound with no new directory, no credential provisioning, and no change to where transcripts and memory live, so the existing "Clearing memory" step stays as written. Isolation is only as complete as the flags' current coverage, which must be verified against each host version and can change under an auto-updating host, and the residue the flags leave still differs between machines; the run also still reads and writes the maintainer's config directory, so transcripts and memory of other runs sit beside it, a reach the filesystem-confinement question decides.

Isolation: the harness runs every invocation with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointing at one dedicated benchmark config directory, outside the maintainer's own, that holds no plugins, MCP servers, or hooks, so only the plugin passed by --plugin-dir loads; the same directory is reused across runs. Reproducibility: the directory's settings and its (empty or fixed) CLAUDE.md are a committed template in the inputs area, a shared input versioned by content and recorded in the manifest in place of the user_config digests; the directory is rebuilt from the template whenever the template changes, and the pre-flight asserts it matches the template. Credentials are provisioned into it once, outside the template. Shuts out every user-level extension at the root rather than one flag at a time, makes the configuration recreatable on any machine from the repository alone, and needs a login only once. A reused directory accumulates state between runs: the host writes transcripts, caches, and possibly settings into it, so drift and other runs' transcripts sit inside the very directory each run loads, and the "Clearing memory" step must move to the new location; and how far a separate OS user or machine already provides this is a condition the filesystem-confinement question settles.

Isolation: the harness creates a new config directory for each run from a committed template and points every invocation of that run (replies and planned-turn answer invocations included) at it through CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR; it holds no plugins, MCP servers, or hooks, so only the plugin passed by --plugin-dir loads. Reproducibility: the template is a shared input in the inputs area, versioned by content and recorded in the manifest in place of the user_config digests, so changing it starts a new comparison set under the existing rule. Credentials are injected per run from outside the template (an API key in the environment or a copied login), and the directory is deleted with the clone after the Run: commit. Strongest isolation and reproducibility a config-level measure gives: every run starts from byte-identical configuration recreatable anywhere from the repository, with no drift and no other run's transcripts or memory inside its config directory, which also makes the memory-clearing step a consequence of the fresh directory rather than a separate check. Per-run credential provisioning is new harness work and a new place for a secret to leak into a record, the host may treat each fresh directory as a first launch (onboarding or trust prompts a headless run must get past), and the template has to be maintained against host releases; how far a separate OS user or machine already provides this is a condition the filesystem-confinement question settles.

open-question.question: Both Cairn agents and every manual invocation run with web search and fetch enabled, and once the Pages site and the run branches are public a web search for the project's name finds earlier artifacts and the repository holding the hidden requirements. Are web search and fetch tools disallowed in scenario invocations?
open-question.alternative: Web search and fetch stay enabled in every scenario invocation, as the draft has them now: the harness adds no tool restriction and no network restriction, and nothing records or checks what a run reached on the web. The draft states this as a decision, never revisited, rather than leaving it unsaid. Every scenario runs with the tool set a real user of the host has, so the benchmark measures Cairn and manual prompting as they are actually used, and the harness carries no extra flag or environment to keep identical across scenarios. Once the Pages site and the run branches are public, a web search for "Closest Wins" can reach earlier artifacts and the repository holding the hidden requirements, so a run can meet a hidden requirement by reading it rather than by surfacing it, the hidden axis stops measuring what it claims, and the effect grows over a campaign and goes unseen. How much is reachable depends on what the sibling question on public inputs leaking decides is published.

Web search and fetch stay enabled in every scenario invocation, but after each run the harness reads the session's tool calls (web search queries, fetched URLs, and shell commands that reach the network) and records them in the run's unpublished record; a run whose calls reached the benchmark repository, its run branches, or its Pages site is marked contaminated, and the draft states whether such a run is excluded from its comparison set or re-run. Runs keep the tool set real users have while contamination becomes visible and countable rather than silent, so a reader can see how often models reach for the web and the analysis can drop the runs that read what they should not have. Detection comes after the run's tokens are spent and needs a matching rule for what counts as reaching the benchmark, which a search result snippet that leaks the hidden topic without any fetch slips past; the tool calls live in the session transcript rather than in the JSON the invocation prints, so the harness gains a transcript reader, and excluding runs makes a set's run count depend on model behaviour.

The harness adds `--disallowedTools WebSearch,WebFetch` to every scenario invocation it sends into a clone (each delivery line, each operator-driven reply, and each planned-turn answer invocation), set in the one place the harness sets every other flag and identical across scenarios; nothing restricts the network otherwise, and nothing audits what a run reached. One flag, set once in the harness and identical for every scenario, removes the tools through which a model would discover earlier artifacts and the hidden requirements, at no cost to the run's machine or environment, and it keeps the difference between scenarios attributable to their definitions. A shell command run under `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (curl, git clone, a package manager) still reaches the web, so the closure is of the easy path only, unchecked; the flag must be confirmed to bind the subagents Cairn's two agents run as, since they declare no tool restriction of their own; and runs no longer use the tool set real users have, so a model cannot check its quiz questions' numeric answers against a source.

The harness adds `--disallowedTools WebSearch,WebFetch` to every scenario invocation it sends into a clone, identical across scenarios, and after each run reads the session's shell commands for network access, recording them in the run's unpublished record and marking a run whose commands reached the benchmark repository, its run branches, or its Pages site as contaminated, with the draft stating whether such a run is excluded or re-run; the network itself is not restricted. The flag shuts the direct path cheaply while the audit catches the shell workaround the flag leaves open, so the remaining leak is both rare and visible, without needing a network-restricted machine. The harness gains both a flag and a transcript reader with a matching rule for network-reaching shell commands, which an indirect command (a script the agent wrote, a package that downloads) can evade; detection still comes after the run is paid for, and the subagent-binding and real-use costs of the flag remain.

Every scenario invocation runs in an environment whose outbound network is limited to the model provider's API endpoint, so web search, fetch, shell commands, and package managers all fail to reach anything else, and the harness also adds `--disallowedTools WebSearch,WebFetch` so models do not spend turns on calls that would fail; the egress rule is part of the harness, identical across scenarios, and the draft states it beside the flags. It closes every path from a run to the web, not only the two tools, so no run can read the hidden requirements or an earlier artifact online however it tries, and the guarantee holds without inspecting what a run did. It needs a network-controllable execution environment, so its viability depends on the machine and confinement the sibling question on filesystem reach settles and on what the sibling question on the execution environment records; it also stops a run from downloading a library or tool it might vendor into its artifact, which shapes what every scenario can build, and the allowlist must track the provider's endpoints.

open-question.question: From its clone an agent can read the benchmark checkout, whose inputs area holds the hidden-requirement statements, the sibling clones in the shared scratch directory, and other runs' session transcripts under the host's projects directory, and the maintainer's notes record that Docker Desktop blocks these runs on the development machine. What confinement keeps a run from reading the benchmark checkout, other clones, and other runs' transcripts, and on what machine do runs then execute?
open-question.alternative: Confinement: none. Runs keep executing as the maintainer's own user on the development Mac, as the draft's "One run" now describes, with no audit of what a session read. The draft rejects the gap with its reason stated: it names the benchmark checkout, the sibling clones under the shared scratch directory, and the host's projects directory as readable from a clone, and records this as a known threat to validity in "Repository layout and isolation". It may say whether the rejection is permanent or deferred to the benchmark repository's implementation. Costs nothing and needs no machine, runtime, or tooling that has not been tested; the draft stays implementable on the maintainer's Mac exactly as written, and the threat is at least disclosed rather than hidden. A run can read the hidden-requirement statements in the inputs area or another scenario's finished clone and nothing would show it, so the hidden axis and every cross-scenario difference rest on the agent not looking, against the draft's own rule that blindness and isolation are properties of what each party is handed, not of discipline.

Confinement: none at run time; runs execute as the maintainer's user on the development Mac. Enforcement is after the fact: once each invocation ends, the harness reads that session's transcript (every tool call with its path and command) and checks it against an allowed set, the clone and the plugin checkout; any read, glob, grep, or shell command touching the benchmark checkout, another clone, or the projects directory voids the run, which is recorded with the reason and excluded from scoring, a rule the draft states beside the pre-flight. Works on the existing machine with no sandbox, OS user, or container, so the Docker Desktop situation never matters, and it produces positive evidence for each scored run that it stayed inside its clone. Detection only: a shell command can reach a path indirectly (a variable, a parent-directory walk, a script it wrote), so a clean audit is not proof, and the voiding rule turns contamination into lost runs and their spent tokens; the transcripts it reads sit in the projects directory whose location the host-configuration sibling decides.

Confinement: the coding host's own controls on the development Mac. The harness runs every invocation with the host's sandboxed shell restricted to the clone (plus read-only access to the plugin checkout) and with permission deny rules for the file-reading tools on the benchmark checkout, the scratch directory's other entries, and the projects directory, carried in a settings file the harness passes; the harness keeps a transcript audit as a backstop, since the boundary is enforced by the program under test. No separate user, container, or machine. Closest to the draft as written: one machine, one user, a per-run settings value the harness already owns, and no new infrastructure to describe or maintain. The boundary is enforced by the agent harness being measured, so a gap in its sandbox or rule matching is a gap in the benchmark; the maintainer's notes record that a shell-granting sandboxed run is exactly what Docker Desktop's stock files block on this Mac, so this may not run here at all, and whether deny rules hold under the permission-skipping flag every invocation uses must be checked before the draft relies on it.

Confinement: operating-system file permissions on the development Mac. Every invocation runs as a dedicated unprivileged benchmark user; the benchmark checkout and the maintainer's home are unreadable to it, each clone is created owned by that user with no group or other access, and the user's own home holds its own host configuration and projects directory. Isolation between runs relies on that user's state per run: other clones and earlier transcripts are moved out of its reach or deleted before the next invocation. No container and no second machine. A real OS-enforced boundary for the benchmark checkout and the hidden requirements, independent of the program under test, on the machine the maintainer already has and without touching Docker. All runs share one user, so keeping one run from reading another's clone or transcript depends on per-run cleanup and on runs not overlapping, which ties it to the concurrent-runs sibling; the harness needs privilege escalation to switch users, and the user's tools, browsers, and credentials must be provisioned separately on a machine that also does daily work.

Confinement: one fresh container per run on the development Mac, through a container runtime other than Docker Desktop's (or Docker Desktop itself, if a check shows the recorded blocker concerns only the host's own shell sandbox and not a containerized headless invocation). The container mounts only that run's clone read-write and the plugin checkout read-only, has its own home so its projects directory is its own, and is discarded after the run; the harness and the operator stay outside it on the Mac. Each run sees only its clone by construction, so the benchmark checkout, sibling clones, and other runs' transcripts are all out of reach regardless of what the agent tries or how runs overlap, while the campaign stays on the maintainer's own machine. Rests on an untested premise, that the Docker Desktop blocker does not extend to a container runtime on this Mac; the run then executes on a Linux image rather than macOS, so the image becomes an input whose OS, tools, and browsers must be stated (the execution-environment sibling's axis), and the host's credentials must be passed into each container.

Confinement: one fresh container per run, as in the Mac container option (only the clone read-write, the plugin checkout read-only, a container-own home and projects directory, discarded after the run), executed on a dedicated Linux machine or Linux VM rather than the development Mac. The harness, the benchmark checkout, and the operator run on that host outside the containers; the Mac only starts campaigns and reads results. Strong per-run isolation on a platform where the container and shell-sandbox tooling is known to work, sidestepping the Docker Desktop blocker entirely and leaving the maintainer's machine and configuration out of every run. Needs a Linux machine to be provisioned, paid for or maintained, and kept as a stated environment for the whole campaign, plus the host's credentials on it; nothing in the project has run there yet, so the draft commits to infrastructure that exists only on paper.

Confinement: a whole virtual machine per run. The harness, kept on a controller (the Mac or a server), creates a fresh VM (a cloud instance or a hosted CI runner job) holding only the run's clone, the plugin checkout, and the host binary, drives every invocation in it remotely, collects the outputs and the branch, and destroys the VM; the benchmark checkout and the operator never exist on the run's machine. The strongest boundary on offer: nothing of the benchmark, other runs, or any shared configuration is present on the machine where the agent works, and each run's environment starts from the same image, which also helps reproducibility on another machine. The most infrastructure and the slowest per run: image building, remote control, credential handling per VM, and per-run machine cost, all of it a harness the draft must specify before a single run; a hosted CI runner also ties execution to that service's limits and images.

open-question.question: Nothing states what OS, tools on PATH, and browsers a run finds, though these shape what every scenario can build and what the rater can drive. Is the execution environment declared as a versioned shared input of a comparison set, recorded in the manifest only, or left unrecorded?
open-question.alternative: The run environment (OS and version, the tools on PATH with their versions, the installed browsers) is written as one environment definition under the inputs area, versioned by content under an id like the operator definition, and listed among the shared inputs; the pre-flight probes the live machine and refuses the run when it does not match the definition, the manifest records the definition's id, and a change to the definition starts a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing beyond what the seed's CLAUDE.md already says, and the rater's browser stays in the rater definition as now. Puts the environment under the same rule as every other input that shapes results (byte-identical across scenarios, recorded by content, a change never mixed into a comparison), and gives a later re-run on another machine a target it can be checked against rather than a guess. Every probed version has to be held still for a whole campaign, so auto-updating browsers and tools must be pinned or disabled and a drifted machine refuses runs until reprovisioned; whether the pin can be enforced depends on the machine and confinement the filesystem-reach question settles, and whether a change starts a new set rests on the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

The environment is declared inside the seed's CLAUDE.md, which the draft already calls an environment description: it names the OS, the tools on PATH, and the browsers a run finds, so the seed tag versions the declaration and no separate input or manifest field is added; the pre-flight probes the machine against the same list and refuses on a mismatch, and a change to the environment is a change to the seed and starts a new comparison set through the seed tag. The run agent reads the declaration; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Adds no new kind of input and no new versioning path, and every scenario learns equally what it can use (for example that no package manager is present), so no run spends turns discovering the machine or builds against a tool that is absent. Any environment change, even a browser patch release, bumps the seed tag, which invalidates every phase-1 run as a parent for phase 2 and moves the trend's seed line; and telling the agent which tools exist shapes what each scenario builds, turning a measurement condition into part of the prompt every run reads.

The environment is declared as an environment definition under the inputs area, as a provisioning target rather than a set-defining input; the harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records the observed OS, PATH tool versions, and browsers in an environment field of the manifest beside the definition's id, and a mismatch with the definition is flagged by the analysis step and reported beside the affected rows rather than refusing the run or starting a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing new; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Gives another machine a stated target to reproduce while letting a campaign that spans days absorb a browser or tool auto-update without discarding the set, with every deviation visible in the record instead of hidden. A flagged mismatch still sits inside one comparison, so a difference between scenarios can be partly the environment's, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions; the analysis must decide per flag whether it matters, which is a judgment the rest of the design avoids. Whether drift may stay inside a set is the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

No environment is declared. The harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records what it finds (OS and version, a fixed list of tools on PATH with their versions, installed browsers) in an environment field of each run's manifest; the environment is not a shared input, a change starts no new comparison set, and the analysis may group or compare runs by the recorded values after the fact. The rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Costs one probe and one manifest field, needs no provisioning or pinning, and still leaves a record from which any later question about what a run found can be answered. Records without controlling: runs on two machines or across an update mix silently within a set unless someone reads the field, a later re-run has nothing to reproduce but a list of observed versions, and the fixed probe list misses any tool a run reached that the list did not name.

The environment is neither declared nor recorded: a run finds whatever the machine running the harness has, and the draft states this choice with its reason (all scenarios of a campaign run on one machine, so the environment is common to them) instead of leaving it unsaid. Nothing to build, pin, or maintain, and within one campaign on one unchanged machine every scenario does meet the same environment. Results cannot be reproduced or audited elsewhere, and a tool or browser update during a campaign, or a move to another machine (which the filesystem-reach question may require), changes what scenarios can build with no trace, mixed into the trend as if it were a plugin change.

open-question.question: A Cairn skill that stops on its own precondition prints a message and exits 0, so the harness, which stops the chain only on a non-zero exit, carries on past it and can record a chain that closed an empty milestone as every invocation made. By what signal does the harness detect that an invocation stopped on a skill's own check rather than completing?

Each skill's success line is fixed and identifier-free, but apart from the bootstrap's no-op line the no-op and precondition-stop messages are prose whose wording the files only exemplify, so a harness matching final messages can recognize success but not which stop occurred. Does Cairn fix the wording of every skill's no-op and stop lines in this milestone?
open-question.alternative: Cairn's skills are not changed in this milestone. Every no-op and stop message keeps its current form: prose whose wording the SKILL.md files only exemplify, with the bootstrap's `Workflow already bootstrapped — nothing changed.` the one fixed exception. The draft states that a harness can recognize only the fixed success lines, so any final message that is not one counts as "not a success", with which stop it was left unclassified or read by hand from the run record. The fix is left for a later Cairn milestone, or never made. No runtime file, host rebuild, or test changes. The draft already keeps where a chain stopped as unscored record read by hand, and success against non-success is enough to find the first invocation that did not complete. The manifest cannot say which stop ended a chain (a derive refusal, an empty task list, a no-op finish), so telling a behavioural stop from a model's improvised message needs a person. Whether this is enough depends on the signal the sibling stop-detection question settles on. The same prose stop can also be worded differently from run to run, which weakens comparison across runs.

Every skill's no-op and stop messages open with one of a small fixed set of identifier-free class prefixes, for example one for "nothing changed" and one for "stopped on a precondition". The rest of the line, and any lines after it, stay free prose, including variable detail such as Short Titles or a tool's `Error:` line. Each SKILL.md's reporting step states the prefix, and the set is listed once in `docs/skill-reference.md`. Nothing tests that the prefixes appear. A small, uniform edit across all skills that lets a harness sort each final message into success, no-op, or stop with one match, without fixing dozens of individual lines. The harness can tell that a stop happened but not which one, so the question's aim of recognizing which stop occurred is only half met. Nothing catches a later edit that drops or rewords a prefix.

The same fixed class prefixes as above, on every skill's no-op and stop messages, with free prose after them. They are also pinned by a test in the pytest suite that reads the rendered skill files and fails when a reporting step no longer carries its listed prefix, or when the list in `docs/skill-reference.md` drifts from the skill files. The success / no-op / stop sorting becomes a checked contract that a benchmark harness can depend on across Cairn versions, at the cost of a single small test. It still cannot say which stop occurred. It also adds a test that scrapes runtime prose, a kind of check the suite has so far kept only for the answer sweep's fixed shell calls, and every later change to a reporting step must keep that test passing.

Only the skills the draft's chains invoke get fixed wording: bootstrap, define, goto, starting-state, review, the two annotating passes, the answer skills and sweep, derive, complete-all-tasks, and finish. Each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition in them gets its own fixed, identifier-free first line, unique across the plugin. Variable detail (the titles derive-tasks lists, the sweep's stopped-at Short Title, a quoted `Error:` line) moves to the lines after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`. Skills outside the chains keep example wording, and nothing tests the lines. A harness matching final messages can name exactly which stop ended a chain. The edit is limited to the skills the benchmark actually exercises, which keeps this milestone's runtime change and its rebuild bounded. The plugin ends up with two reporting conventions, one for chain skills and one for the rest, so a skill that later joins a chain needs the same work redone. Nothing guards the fixed lines against drift, so a later wording edit silently breaks the harness's classification.

The same scope and form as the chain-skills option: a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each no-op and precondition stop in the chain skills, with variable detail on later lines and the list in `docs/skill-reference.md`. A pytest test also checks each listed line verbatim against the rendered skill files and checks that no two stops share a line. Skills outside the chains keep example wording. Exact stop identification for every skill the benchmark runs, as a contract checked on every commit, so a harness built against one Cairn version keeps classifying correctly on the next. The work stays limited to the chain skills. Two reporting conventions remain. The new prose-scraping test must be maintained, and it fails on any rewording of a chain skill's stop step, which slows ordinary edits to those skills.

Every skill in the plugin, inside and outside the chains (capture, submit-task, complete-task, modify-milestone-goal, and the rest included), gets a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition, with variable detail on the lines after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant is extended from success lines to them. Nothing tests the lines. One uniform reporting rule across the whole plugin, matching the existing fixed-success-line invariant, so every stop in any chain, present or future, can be identified by its line. The largest runtime edit of the prose options, touching every SKILL.md's reporting step and requiring a host rebuild, most of it for skills no benchmark chain runs. Nothing guards the lines against drift.

Every skill gets a fixed, unique, identifier-free first line for each distinct no-op and precondition-stop condition, with variable detail after it. The lines are listed in `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant is extended to them. A pytest test checks each listed line verbatim against the rendered skill files and checks that every line is unique. The complete, checked contract: any final message of any skill can be classified exactly, and a rewording cannot reach a release without the test failing. The most work in this milestone: every reporting step is edited, the hosts are rebuilt, and a new prose-scraping test is added and must be maintained. It also turns reporting wording across the whole plugin into a frozen interface that every later skill edit must respect, largely for the benefit of one benchmark harness.

open-question.question: finish-current-milestone closes a milestone whenever TASKS_TODO.md holds no section, so a chain whose derivation line refused to run finishes an empty milestone, clears the pointer, and leaves a tree that looks like a completed chain. Should the finish skill refuse to close a milestone that recorded no completed task?

An early stop is counted as a result, which also covers a usage limit, an API overload, or a network error reaching an invocation as a failed call, and Cairn spends the most tokens so is the likeliest to hit them. What does the harness do with an invocation that ends in an infrastructure failure rather than in the model's own stop?

No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?

A new rating writes new browser tests for every checklist line, so two ratings of one artifact can test the same line at different strictness, and the draft's claim that a second rating gets the same number holds only for re-running an existing test. What must a rater version pass before it may rate a comparison set, and what is the acceptance rule?

The lost count compares two independent ratings, the parent's and the child's, so rater noise shows as lines lost or gained when nothing changed, and no agreement figure is reported anywhere. Is a sample of each comparison set's artifacts rated twice with the agreement reported beside the scores, and at what sample size?

Each checklist line names a behaviour and nothing more, so a weak test (an undo button exists) and a strict one (the award is actually reversed) both satisfy it. Does each line carry a short specification of the case its test must drive and what it must assert?
open-question.alternative: Every test line (prompt 1's six stated and thirteen implied lines, prompt 2's stated line and eleven implied lines, and prompt 2's carry-between-profiles hidden line) gets a short specification written now into the draft's project section beside the line. The specification names the case the test must drive the artifact into and the observable outcome it must assert, stated as an outcome rather than a means, so the "any way through counts" rule still holds: for the award line, award a point, take it back, and assert the score is back to its earlier value, with a confirmation that prevents the award counting as well. The specification becomes part of the checklist, which stays derived from the draft and nothing else, and keeps the line's id. Pins the strictness of every test line at the one source the checklist is already derived from, so two ratings of one artifact test the same case with the same assertion and the specs are reviewed in the open within this milestone. Roughly thirty-two specs have to be written and agreed now, which lengthens the project section considerably, and an outcome stated too narrowly can fail a legitimate way through that the line's wording meant to accept.

alternative.id: Spec form in draft, specs at implementation

open-question.alternative: The draft adds the rule that every test line carries a specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert, gives its form and one or two worked examples, and changes the derivation rule so the checklist is the draft's lines plus specifications authored in the benchmark repository's inputs area when the checklist is first built. The per-line specifications are not written in this milestone. Settles the design point (each line carries a spec) within the milestone's goal of finalizing the draft, without writing every spec before the harness, the rater, and an artifact to try them on exist. The checklist stops being derived from the draft alone, and until the specs are written nothing pins strictness; whether they are fixed before scored runs depends on the input-freeze question.

The checklist lines stay behaviour-only as the draft has them; each test line's specification of the case to drive and the outcome to assert lives in the rater definition, beside its fixed rating guideline, so it is part of the rater version that every rating file names and the analysis groups by. A sharpened or corrected spec is a new rater version, never a change to the checklist, so line ids and the checklist's derivation stay untouched and ratings made under different specs never mix. What a line means is split across two inputs, and a spec change regroups every earlier rating under an older rater version rather than being re-rated against the same checklist; how a rater version is gated depends on the rater-calibration question.

Only the test lines where a weak and a strict test plainly diverge (an award taken back, a reload surviving, a skip keeping its place, a tie settled, edits not lost, the carry between profiles) get a short case-and-assertion specification in the draft's project section; the remaining lines stay behaviour-only. Spends the writing where the variance actually arises and keeps lines whose test has one obvious form, such as the file opening from disk, as short as they are. Choosing which lines are ambiguous is itself a judgment, so a weak test the selection did not foresee still passes on an unspecified line.

alternative.id: One strictness rule in the guideline

open-question.alternative: No per-line specification. The rater's fixed rating guideline gains one general rule applied to every test line: a test must drive the artifact into the case the line names and assert the resulting state, never only the presence of a control, label, or button. Closes the named failure (a test that only finds an undo button) with one sentence that also covers lines added later, at no cost to the checklist's length. Leaves to each rating what the resulting state is for each line, so two strict tests can still assert different outcomes and disagree on the same artifact.

Nothing is added to the checklist lines or the rating guideline; a line keeps naming a behaviour only, and variance in test strictness is left to be caught by whatever checks of the rater the benchmark adopts. Keeps the checklist exactly as short and as derivable as it is now, and adds no input to write, freeze, or version. Two ratings of one artifact can still test a line at different strictness, which also shows as lost or gained lines in phase 2 when nothing changed; whether that is caught at all depends on the rater-calibration and repeat-rating questions.

open-question.question: A test line the rater could not drive the artifact to scores zero like a missing behaviour, with the not-proved count reported beside the axis, which penalises an artifact a browser test finds hard to drive (a canvas-based UI) regardless of what a host could do with it. How is a not-proved line scored?

The rater receives the entry file and the files it loads, so an editor page reached only by a link or a saved set file beside the HTML never reaches it and every line about it fails as not proved. What part of a run's tree does the rater receive?

The run script detects a root index.html, and a run that put its entry elsewhere gets the manifest's entry field by hand, against the rule that nothing about a run is done by hand and by a person who sees the manifest's scenario. How is a run's entry point determined when it is not a root index.html?

The reference strategy models_strategy_1 is said to be written from Cairn's own usage snippets, but only three of its twelve rows match docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, which assigns Opus at high to the bootstrap, define, goto, and finish lines, Fable at high to the starting-state, review, recommend, and derive lines, and Opus at xhigh to task completion. Which of the two changes to match the other, or do they diverge with the "as it is used" claim dropped?

docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md repeats the review pass until it reports convergence, raises the review line to a stronger model for a stuck milestone, and re-runs task completion after a usage-limit stop, none of which a fixed message list can express, and the YOLO chain runs the review once. Does the delivery model gain a bounded loop (a named span of lines repeated up to a declared count until the review line prints its convergence verdict), with the bound part of the delivery?

The define line records "Carry out the task described in PROJECT.md." verbatim as milestone 1's goal, and phase 2 overwrites that file, so from then on the recorded goal points at prompt 2 and the phase-2 starting-state pass reads a milestone whose goal no longer describes what it built. What text does the define line carry as the milestone goal?

Phase 1 is run for every scenario "as many times as the set calls for", with no number set and no stopping rule, so a margin between two scenarios can be noise. How many runs per scenario does a comparison set require?

The ranking table has a runs column but no spread or interval beside any score, so a reader cannot tell a margin between two scenarios from noise. Is a per-run spread or interval reported beside every score, and where?

The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?

Each family's radar curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the best of several noisy scores is biased upward, more so for Cairn, which has many configurations (versions times strategies) where manual has few. Which scenario is each family's radar curve drawn from?

The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?

A comparison set is one seed tag and one version of each prompt, yet an operator change must also start a new set, the analysis groups by rater version, and the host CLI auto-updates across a campaign that spans several days. Which versions define a comparison set?

Nothing lists which scenarios a comparison set must contain, so "complete" is undefined and the strongest manual strategy can be left out while the radar claims to compare against it. Does a comparison set declare a roster of scenarios that must all be rated before it counts as complete, and what must the roster hold?

The published trend follows per-scenario aggregates across comparison sets and plugin commits, so a change to the inputs and a change to the plugin are mixed in one line, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions. How does the trend continue when a shared input changes?

Phase 2 starts as soon as the parent's Run: commit exists, which implies runs in parallel, yet every run's pre-flight requires the benchmark checkout to be on a clean main and every run commits to it. Are runs sequential, or how do concurrent runs share the benchmark checkout?

Each hidden requirement's evidence must settle the question once asked while the prompt alone gives no reason to ask, and nothing has tested this: prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" may already invite the topic question, and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" sits close to the export convention. What procedure and acceptance rule calibrate each prompt's hidden requirement before scored runs?

The animal reading line scores the count of animal questions out of ten, which is undefined for an artifact that holds more than ten questions or draws ten per game. How is that line scored for such an artifact?

"About an animal" has borderline items, such as the zoo's visitor count or how many animals live at the zoo, while a reading line promises one defensible answer per item. Does the hidden-requirement entry state a classification rule for borderline items?

The benchmark's main branch is public, so the hidden requirements, the operator records, and every artifact are public and future models will train on them, wearing down the no-canned-solution requirement over time. How does the benchmark limit or account for its inputs and results leaking into training data?

Each prompt's checklist is derived from the draft's project section, which no version pins, and nothing freezes the checklist and hidden requirements before a comparison set's first scored run. Are the checklist and hidden-requirement entries frozen before the first scored run of a set, and how?

The README shows only the latest complete comparison set, so a seed bump replaces a bad result on the landing page with no trace. Does the page keep superseded comparison sets linked with the reason each was superseded?

The operator's input is the prompt text as committed, which in phase 2 is prompt 2 alone, so a phase-2 question about the game's existing flow reaches a stakeholder who does not know the game they asked for in phase 1. Which prompts does the operator receive in phase n?

The ranking-table section opens by saying the table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches, while the radar text says the page states no claim the data does not. Does that sentence change to say the table shows whether Cairn beats them?

Every gap in ideas/benchmark_design_gaps.md is to end as a decision in the draft, and the report's Where references are line numbers that shift with every edit of the draft. What happens to the report once its gaps are resolved?

The draft's examples name Cairn 1.8.3 and a host binary 2.1.283 while this repository's VERSION reads 1.9.0, and it says docs/design-claims.md states that only one claim is tested where that document now says two. Are such facts refreshed to the current state in this milestone, or rewritten so the draft no longer states a fact that moves?
